nameStory: The name "gutweed" comes from this seaweed's hollow, tube-like structure that resembles intestines when you hold it up to the light. It's also called "green bait weed" because fishermen have long used its bright green strands to attract fish.
description: Gutweed is a bright green marine algae that forms hollow, inflated tubes along New England's rocky shores. These squishy, finger-like structures can grow up to a foot long and feel like deflated balloons when you squeeze them. Unlike flat seaweeds, gutweed's tubular shape makes it look almost like green sausages attached to rocks. It's actually a type of sea lettuce, despite looking quite different from its flatter relatives.

idTips.label: Hollow tubes
idTips.description: The entire plant consists of bright green, inflated tubes that feel squishy and balloon-like when gently squeezed - you can actually feel the water and air inside

idTips.label: Attachment point
idTips.description: Multiple tubes emerge from a small, disc-like holdfast (root-like structure) that grips tightly to rocks and shells

idTips.label: Translucent walls
idTips.description: Hold a tube up to the light and you can see through the thin walls - they're almost transparent with a fresh, sea-lettuce smell

idTips.label: Bright green color
idTips.description: Vibrant emerald green when fresh and underwater, becoming duller olive-green when dried by low tide

idTips.label: Clustered growth
idTips.description: Often grows in dense patches with dozens of tubes waving together in the current like underwater grass

habitat: Look for gutweed in the intertidal zone along New England's rocky coastlines, particularly in tide pools and on wave-exposed rocks. It thrives in areas with good water circulation and can tolerate both full marine conditions and slightly brackish water near river mouths. You'll often find it growing alongside barnacles, mussels, and other hardy intertidal species.

seasonality.spring: New growth begins as tiny green tubes emerging from holdfast. This is when the tubes are most tender and brightest green.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season with full-sized, robust tubes that are easy to spot at low tide. The hollow structures are most inflated and squishy during this time.
seasonality.fall: Still present and identifiable, though older tubes may start to look more weathered and darker. New growth may appear after summer die-back.
seasonality.winter: Many tubes break off in winter storms, but the holdfast survives. Look for shorter, more stubby tubes that have weathered the harsh conditions.

funFact: Scientists used to think gutweed belonged to a completely different genus called Enteromorpha (which literally means "intestine-shaped"), until DNA analysis in the early 2000s revealed it was actually a tubular cousin of the flat sea lettuces all along!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other tubular seaweeds, but gutweed's bright green color and truly hollow, inflated tubes set it apart from stringier, solid algae. Memory trick: if you can squeeze it like a balloon and it feels hollow, it's probably gutweed.
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the name "kelp" in one of its alternate names (grass kelp) fool you - this isn't a true kelp at all, but rather a much simpler green algae. True kelps are large brown seaweeds, while this is a delicate green species.
compareHints: Unlike its flat relative Broadleaf Sea Lettuce which looks like green tissue paper, gutweed forms distinctive hollow tubes. Green String Lettuce is also tubular but much narrower and less inflated, while Thread Weed has flattened, ribbon-like branches rather than round, balloon-like tubes.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Broadleaf Sea Lettuce differs from its relatives by forming broad, flat sheets rather than tubes or ribbons.
Green String Lettuce differs from Broadleaf Sea Lettuce by its narrow ribbon shape rather than broad, flat sheets.
Thread Weed differs from Broadleaf Sea Lettuce by being much narrower and more compressed rather than broad and flat.
